01.actor: Rav Aha bar Yaakov (and the sixty elders of Rav Huna's study hall)
01.event: Rav Aha bar Yaakov was afflicted by suskhinta from holding back during Rav Huna's long discourses
01.turn: They suspended him from the cedar column of the study hall and a green substance came out of him
01.outcome: He was healed and, alone of sixty elders, did not become impotent
01.summary: Many of Rav Huna's students became impotent from holding back during his long discourses. Rav Aha bar Yaakov fell ill from the same cause; he was hung from the cedar column of the study hall, a green substance came out of him, and he was cured. He later said that of sixty elders he alone escaped impotence, by this remedy.
01.reason: Rav Aha's affliction, the cure applied to him and its result are narrated actions with a change, beyond a bare report of what happened to the others.

02.missing: Any narrated incident; the segment is an inference from a verse about the Israelites offering the omer before eating, inside a legal argument.
02.reason: A legal inference from a biblical verse, not a narrated event; even as narrative it would concern biblical figures.

03.actor: A certain man and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
03.event: A man testified that someone had established presumptive Levite status by reading second in the synagogue
03.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi questioned him whether the reading was as a Levite or as a prominent man
03.outcome: On his testimony, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi elevated the person to Levite status
03.summary: A man came before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and testified that someone had read second in the synagogue, after a priest. After questioning him, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi elevated that person to Levite status on his word.
03.missing: Any action or change besides the testimony before the rabbi and his ruling.
03.reason: A case brought before a rabbi, a question and answer, and a ruling; under R-C0's limit (2026-10-25) coming before the rabbi and being ruled on is not a story.

04.event: Engrossed in his learning, he wandered beyond his Shabbat limit
04.turn: Rav Hisda told Rav Nahman his student was in distress
04.outcome: Rav Nahman instructed that a human partition be made so he could reenter
04.summary: Nehemya was so absorbed in study that he walked beyond the Shabbat limit without noticing and was stranded. Rav Hisda brought his plight to Rav Nahman, who told him to form a partition of people so Nehemya could walk back in.
04.missing: That the partition was actually formed and Nehemya returned is not stated.
04.reason: One real event (straying beyond the limit) followed by a ruling whose outcome is only implied; more than a bare case before a rabbi, so borderline rather than not.

05.missing: Any event beyond Rabbi Zeira arriving in Eretz Yisrael and hearing Rabbi Asi teach a ruling.
05.reason: A setting that only frames the transmission of a halakha; teaching is speech and there is no conflict or change.

06.event: Rava poured drinks for guests at his son's wedding; some sages stood for him and two did not
06.outcome: He rebuked them: are these sages and those not sages?
06.summary: At his son's wedding Rava served the guests himself. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna stood when he poured for them, but Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas did not, and Rava grew angry and rebuked them.
06.reason: Narrated actions (serving, standing, not standing), an emotional reaction and conflict make an event that happened, not a hypothetical.

07.event: A man came before Rabbi Yosei and asked about halitza within three months
07.turn: Rabbi Yosei forbade it and the man pressed him
07.outcome: Rabbi Yosei cited a verse to justify the ruling
07.summary: A man asked Rabbi Yosei whether halitza may be performed within three months of the husband's death. Rabbi Yosei said no, and when challenged he cited a verse.
07.missing: Any action beyond the question, answer and justification.
07.reason: A question and answer before a rabbi with no other event; a setting plus question and answer is not a story.

08.missing: The incident itself; only that Rabba issued a practical ruling on a found get, with disputed details.
08.reason: A bare report that Rabba ruled in a case, cited as evidence of his view, with nothing narrated beyond the ruling.

09.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Hiyya
09.event: Rabbi fell ill and Rabbi Hiyya visited and found him crying
09.turn: Rabbi Hiyya asked why he wept, citing signs that dying while crying is a bad omen
09.outcome: Rabbi answered that he wept for the Torah and mitzvot he would lose
09.summary: When Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi fell ill, Rabbi Hiyya came in and found him crying. He asked why, reminding him that dying in tears is a bad sign, and Rabbi said he was crying over the Torah and mitzvot he could no longer fulfill.
09.missing: Any change or consequence after the exchange.
09.reason: There are real events (illness, a visit, weeping, an emotional reaction) but the passage is mainly dialogue with little change: R-C7 shape 1.

10.event: She refused her husband in his absence
10.outcome: Beit Shammai explain the Sages treated him harshly because he mismanaged her property
10.summary: Beit Hillel cite the case of Pishon's wife refusing him in his absence; Beit Shammai answer that the Sages dealt severely with him because he had dealt dishonestly with her property.
10.missing: The incident is only cited in debate; one act with no narrated change.
10.reason: Jeff ruled this passage (Yevamot 107b) not a story: one thing Pishon's wife did, without change or causality.

11.actor: A woman holding a bag of documents
11.event: Heirs claimed a bag of documents deposited with her; she said she had seized it during the depositor's life
11.turn: They came before Rav Nahman, who asked for witnesses
11.outcome: She had none, so he ruled the seizure was after death and void
11.summary: A woman held a bag of documents on deposit. When the heirs demanded it she claimed to have seized it from the deceased for a debt while he lived. Rav Nahman asked for witnesses, she had none, and he ruled the seizure ineffective.
11.missing: Any event after the case reached court beyond questioning and ruling.
11.reason: There are events before the court (deposit, the heirs' claim, her seizure), but after she comes to court it is all dialogue and a ruling; between borderline and not, borderline.

12.actor: A widow at Rabbi Yehuda's court
12.event: A woman came to Rabbi Yehuda's court to testify to her husband's death
12.turn: Those present told her to lament, tear her clothes and loosen her hair
12.summary: A woman came to Rabbi Yehuda's court, and the people there advised her to perform mourning so the court would believe her. The Gemara then discusses whether they taught her to lie.
12.missing: Whether she did so and what the court ruled.
12.reason: Coming to court and being given advice is the only event; nothing further is narrated and the rest is legal discussion.

13.actor: Residents of a shepherds' village and Rav Yehuda
13.event: A sea inlet breached a courtyard wall
13.turn: The matter came before Rav Yehuda
13.outcome: He required only one board to permit it
13.summary: Rav Yosef recalls that a sea inlet broke through a courtyard wall in a shepherds' village, and Rav Yehuda, asked about it, required only one standing board.
13.missing: Any action or change besides the case and the ruling.
13.reason: One event followed by a ruling, cited as precedent; Jeff's 2026-10-25 ruling makes this shape not a story.

14.missing: Any event; Shmuel only tells Rav Hana to gather ten men so he can announce a halakha.
14.reason: Speech only, without conflict, cited in a legal argument.

15.actor: The people of the Upper Galilee
15.event: They bought a poor man of noble descent from Tzippori a litra of meat every day
15.summary: The people of the Upper Galilee provided a poor man of good family a litra of meat daily; the Gemara then discusses what was remarkable about it.
15.missing: Any one-time event or consequence following the habitual practice.
15.reason: A habitual practice reported as evidence that leads to nothing, followed by commentary; a custom that leads nowhere stays a custom.

16.event: Rav walked among sheaves and saw them waving
16.outcome: He told them business is better than farming
16.summary: Rav walked through a field and, seeing the sheaves wave, remarked to them that commerce pays better than farming. Rava then gives a dictum on the same theme.
16.missing: Any change or consequence; the act only frames a saying.
16.reason: A setting framing an aphorism, with no conflict or change.

17.missing: Any narrated incident; only a list of sages who had items brought in through human partitions.
17.reason: A bare report of practices cited as precedent, with nothing following.

18.missing: Any event; Rav Dimi only praises his interlocutor's understanding.
18.reason: Speech within scholarly exchange, praise without conflict or event.

19.event: The student became liable to death by burning
19.turn: The Rabbis said to leave him alone
19.outcome: He was spared because he had served a great man
19.summary: A student of Rabbi Eliezer committed a sin deserving burning, but the Rabbis let him go because he had served a great teacher.
19.missing: What he did and how the matter unfolded; the incident is only alluded to.
19.reason: An incident only alluded to, with a ruling that changes his fate; between borderline and not, so borderline.

20.event: A man who had made an eiruv with onions to travel to Tiv'in came before Rabbi Meir in Ardiska
20.turn: Rabbi Meir held an onion eiruv invalid
20.outcome: He made the man stay within his four cubits
20.summary: Rabbi Meir spent Shabbat in Ardiska. A man came to him saying he had set an eiruv with onions to reach Tiv'in, and Rabbi Meir confined him to his four cubits.
20.missing: Any further development beyond the ruling's enforcement.
20.reason: A case before a rabbi, but the ruling is itself an act that changes the man's situation (he is confined), like the 'apportioning' in Ketubot 65a, so borderline.
